chapter_theme: Songs at Palani (பழநி, 6 of 7), many naming the shrine at its foot, Avinankudi: the poet confesses capture by women's charms and by courtesans who take a man's money, and asks for the Lord's feet, for jnana, or simply not to forget him; between these stand a namo-nama litany, a song of kundalini yoga, a positive plea to live by scripture in service, and a self-indictment that lists the virtues he lacks.
structure_note: Confessions of desire (180, 183 to 187, 190, 191, 193), the courtesan's trade named in 180, 183 and 193; birth to infatuation (181); praise only, in litany form (179); a plea for disciplined service (182); the yogic ascent (188); a list of missing virtues with the Sambandar story (189); a brief prayer through the six-syllable mantra (192). 184 gives its whole praise to the Goddess.

179.reading: A litany of praise ending each line with நமோநம: Murugan is hailed as the king who gives teaching, the god in whom justice dwells, the form of the rare Veda mantras, the master of jnana, the one in love with the hunters' creeper and the treasure of the heavenly girl, and is asked for grace. The second half tells how his sharp vel killed sinful Sura so the gods regained heaven, praises Siva of Kailash, and names Uma by many titles, Ambika, Manonmani, Sundari, Narayani, Abhirami, as the mother who fondles him, at the shrine of Avinankudi.
179.nuance: There is no confession here; the song is a string of invocations, a form of worship by naming. போதகந்தரு கோவே and ஞான பண்டித நாதா make Murugan the giver of knowledge, and வேத மந்திர ரூபா makes him the mantra's form. The phrase ஆவல் கொண்டு விறாலே சிராடவெ, apparently the mother's fond play with her son, is unclear.

180.reading: The poet describes women with turmeric-scented breasts who walk the fragrant streets, bend passers-by with their eyes, embrace those who come, state their trade, win full trust and then snatch their wealth, and asks that his mind not wander seeking the houses of these women who sell pleasure, but that Murugan come today, give him abundant love and rule him. The praise names him Uma's son and Kanda the guru, lover of the Kurava girl, whose lotus feet poets worship, and to whom the sage of the southern-breeze mountain bowed in fine Tamil and received grace, on southern Palani.
180.nuance: தொழில்கூறி and விலைமாதர் name the trade plainly: these are women who sell. The plea asks for the Lord's love (அன்புடைமை) to replace theirs. தென்றல்வரை முநிநாதர் is the sage of Pothigai, Agastya, here worshipping Murugan as guru in Tamil, the claim the book repeats that Murugan taught Tamil to Agastya.

181.reading: The poet traces his life from Brahma's sending him out to eat his deeds, through birth, the breast and childhood, to a grown body that enters the houses of common women and spends night and day there until it turns foolish, and asks when, leaving this birth and death bound up with two kinds of deed, he will worship the Lord's paired feet. The praise is given to Vishnu as Murugan's uncle: Rama who walked the dark forest with Sita and whose monkey burned Lanka, and Krishna who saw through Kamsa's tricks and crawled between the marudha trees, and ends at Palani of lotus pools.
181.nuance: The song is a small autobiography of the soul: மருமலரினன் துரந்துவிட, sent off by the one on the flower (Brahma), வினை அருந்த, to consume deeds. பொதுவையர் அகம் are the houses of women common to all. The opening lines (அந்தி மதியொடு பிறந்து முன் பெய்வதையாலே) are hard to divide, and செறிவுடன் றிந்து looks damaged.

182.reading: Unusually, the plea confesses nothing: the poet asks that, free of anxiety and serving Murugan, not straying from the rules of the Manu texts, seeking the meaning the Vedas hold and following the Agamas in order, trampling the sins deeds bring and driving out anger, he walk in joy and come to worship him. The praise names him the one who enters the mind, who pitied the sages and gods who took refuge at his flower feet and defeated Sura with the vel, and who married the Kurava creeper in the millet field, at fertile Palani.
182.nuance: உனக்கடிமையே புரிந்து is service, and it is joined to an orthodox programme: மநுநூல், the Veda and the ஆகமங்கள் முறையாலே. The rhythm makes வகைப்படி மனோரதங்கள் தொகைப்படியினால் இலங்கி hard to construe; it seems to ask that his wishes be fulfilled in due order.

183.reading: In a long chain of phrases each ending in இலே, the poet names what caught him: a woman's flowered hair, the pride of her sweet words, the twist of her cruel heart, her hips and breasts, her coming close uninvited, the net of her eyes, the jingle of her bangles and the pose that snatches great wealth, so that joined to her for a moment he lost his wits and wanders in thought and dream; he asks that, fool and deceiver as he is, he may worship the golden feet with flowers by Murugan's glance. The praise pictures Murugan wearing gold pendants and kadamba garlands and the Tamil of those who call themselves his servants, dwelling in love at Palani.
183.nuance: The anaphora (கொண்டைச் சொருக்கிலே, செருக்கிலே, இருக்கிலே) makes the list itself the snare. கனநிதி பறி அந்தப் பிலுக்கிலே, the pose that plucks away great wealth, marks her as a courtesan. In the praise the devotee's Tamil is one of Murugan's ornaments, worn with rose-water and the kadamba garland. The lines on the mountain and hills before Palani are unclear.

184.reading: The poet describes lovemaking at length, flowers in the hair, nail-marks, sweating faces, reddened eyes, musk on breasts, bodies joined as one life on the couch, bangles ringing, and asks whether this love of rising infatuation will not end. The whole praise is given to the Goddess: Sankari who bore the world, dwelling in devotees' minds and in one half of Siva, the green one, Parai, Ambika beyond day and night, Tripura, Parabrahmi, the faithful wife, the girl born on the mountain, who gave Murugan, Lord at Palani.
184.nuance: The plea is only a question (அன்பு ஒழிந்திடாதோ), asking for no gift. The praise is a hymn to Shakti in her cosmic titles, and Murugan appears only in the last word, தம்பிரானே, which here replaces பெருமாளே. Several compounds in the Goddess's titles (பசங்கியம் பண கரதலி, இரண்டொடு ஒன்று அலர்) are obscure.

185.reading: The poet confesses sinking into women's arms and pleasure, heedless of the world calling him a worthless man, falling headlong and drinking the nectar of their smiles until he perishes, and asks Murugan for jnana, so that he may drink instead the nectar of the Lord's two feet. The praise names him the one whose vel churned the sea, who rode the peacock against the asura army, and the young one whom Siva, said to be beyond speech, holds in his heart as supreme guru, at Palani whose peaks touch the moon.
185.nuance: விழலன் என உலகோர்கள் மொழியும் அது மதியாமல்: he heard the world's blame and ignored it. The two nectars are set against each other, the smile's (நகையமுதம்) and the feet's (இருதாளின் அமுது). உமைகொழுநர் உளமேவு பரமகுரு alludes to Murugan as Siva's teacher without telling the story.

186.reading: The poet describes women whose eyes outdo the deer, the mango slice and the carp, teaching Kama's arts and destroying propriety, and whose sweet speech and sandal-pasted breasts force men into slavery, and asks that he, a foolish, false-minded cheat, be given Murugan's feet to rejoice in. The praise is for Vishnu as uncle, who killed the demon that lifted the mountain, kicked the cart and the marudha trees and drew the bow that felled trees, and for Murugan who freed the gods from prison and makes his peacock walk at Palani.
186.nuance: வலிய அடிமை புகுத்திவிடும்: here அடிமை is bondage to the women, not service to the Lord, the sense the concept adimai names. The eyes are praised by the old conceit of defeating deer, mango and carp. The poet calls himself அசட்டு மனிதன் முழுது புரட்டன, a foolish man and a cheat through and through.

187.reading: In a dense, doubled-consonant rhythm the poet lists a woman's adornments, the pearl tassel and coiled hair, the green mark and jewelled pendant on the forehead, the three-layered bodice, the sweet words, coral lips and poisonous eyes, and asks whether he must go on wandering, caught by such seductresses and their breasts, his life snared and ruined; he asks that his great sorrow be removed and that, with devotion in his mind, he be given the supreme consciousness. The praise names Murugan the master of knowledge, son of the three-eyed Siddha, wearing the red vetchi garland, worshipped with flowers by siddhas of the eight directions, devotees in nishtha and gods at Palani.
187.nuance: The sound is the point: almost every word doubles a hard consonant (முத்துக்குச் சிட்டுக் குப்பி). பற்பல லச்சைக்குட்பட்டு, falling into many shames, names his own disgrace. சிற்பரம் is the supreme of consciousness, and பத்தத்தொடு seems to stand for bhakti; the splitting of many lines is uncertain.

188.reading: A song of yoga: the poet asks that the breath, run through the channels from the root (ida, pingala and the middle way) up the pillar through the six centres, reach the feet of the Supreme in the radiance of Jnana Sadasiva, and that he become one with the nada and the ringing anklets of the dancing foot. The praise names Murugan the son of Siva who bears the trident, deer, axe, drum and Brahma's skull, the vel that reduced Sura to dust, the dancer whose anklets sound through the ages, and the lover of the forest deer-girl, at Palani.
188.nuance: The vocabulary is technical yoga, as in Tirumular: மூலம், பிங்கலை நாடி, வாயு, மூலந்திகழ் தூண் (the spine as pillar), பால் அங்கு இளர் ஆறு (the six centres), ஞான சதாசிவம். The goal is heard, not only seen: the sound of the nada is the anklet of the Lord's dancing foot. The measurements (நாலங்குலம்) and the சிகாரம் of the sixth line are obscure.

189.reading: The poet lists what he lacks, the chanting of the root mantra, giving, love, silence and jnana, and what he has, lust for women, great thirst, transgression and offence and the name of a dumb fool, and confesses he wanders in this body while thinking of falling into the burning hell Kumbhi; he asks for the sharpness to keep company with those of jnana-filled heart. The praise tells of the Jains, their peacock-feather fans burnt, who argued, of the palm leaf that went against the river, the Pandya cured of illness and the deceivers sent to the stake, as Murugan's work, and names him Sankari's son, the jnana master of the Vedas, at Avinankudi.
189.nuance: The opening is a catalogue of negations (ஓதல் இங்கு இலை, ஈவது இங்கு இலை, மோனம் இங்கு இலை, ஞானம் இங்கு இலை) followed by a catalogue of possessions, with மூகன் (dumb one) as his name. The remedy asked is fellowship: ஞான நெஞ்சினர் பால் இணங்கிடு கூர்மை. The praise identifies Murugan with Sambandar, by tradition the saint whose leaf floated against the Vaigai and who cured the Pandya (மாறன்) before the Jains were impaled.

190.reading: The poet describes lovemaking in full detail, loosened hair, thrilling breasts, jingling bangles, sweat, faltering words, drinking the lips' nectar, and says that even lying on that flower-bed he will not forget Murugan's lotus feet. The praise names the vel that crushed Nirudan's chariots and elephants, the guru with form and without, the Kumara who dwells at the top of the sky, and the lover of the Kurava girl at Palani where waterfalls scatter gems over the areca palms.
190.nuance: Unlike most such songs this one does not ask to leave the embrace: துயிலுகினும் அலர்கமல மலரடியை மறவேனே, 'even if I sleep there, I will not forget the feet'. It reads as a vow of remembrance inside desire rather than a plea for escape. நிகழ் அகள சகள குரு names the Lord as both formless and formed.

191.reading: The poet confesses that he described women in the poets' figures, hair as cloud, breasts as lotus buds, smile as jasmine, gait as a swan, waist as a drum, face as the moon, and then melted like wax in a furnace in the union they gave; he asks that he, a fool sunk in the sea of births, be given the Lord's anklet feet. The praise tells how, when poison rose with the nectar from the churned sea and Vishnu, Brahma and Indra cried for refuge, Siva who took it fathered Murugan, whose vel shattered the asuras, who embraced the Kurava girl and was born in the lotus of Saravana, worshipped as supreme guru at Palani.
191.nuance: The confession is partly a poet's: உருவக உரைசெய்து, having made metaphors of women's forms, the very figures the song lists. The list is the stock catalogue of Tamil love poetry, so the poet indicts his own craft. உவகை தரு கலை பல உணர் பிறவியின் உவரி: the sea of births is the place where he learned the many arts of pleasure.

192.reading: A short song asking that the poet, not forgetting to speak Murugan's praise and not wandering in the river of the mind's sorrow, gain fortune in this world and the next through the six-syllable mantra set to song. The praise names Murugan the one who knows Siva's own word, the vel-bearer enthroned on Palani, who withered the asuras and freed the gods.
192.nuance: இசைபயில் ஷடாக்ஷரம், the six syllables practised in music, is the Murugan mantra (by tradition சரவணபவ). இகபர செளபாக்யம் asks for good in both worlds, not release. பசுபதி சிவாக்யம் உணர்வோனே may allude to Murugan knowing the word he taught Siva; the sense of வசனமிக ஏற்றி is uncertain.

193.reading: The poet heaps abuse on deceitful courtesans who torment those who come, talk of love without knowing friendship, show the wonders of passion on the couch, speak harshly, never melt despite sweet words and only act at union, and asks whether he must waste his body delighting in the pleasure they give. The praise tells of Krishna killing Sakatasura sent by Kamsa and climbing the kurundham tree before the cowherd women, as Vishnu, Murugan's uncle, and of Murugan embracing Devayanai and Valli, Lord of Avinankudi and of every hill.
193.nuance: வஞ்சனை மிஞ்சிய மாய வம்பிகள், இன்சொல் புரிந்து உருகாத தொண்டிகள், சங்கமம் என்பதையே புரிந்தவர்: the deceit is that the sweet words and the union are performance. The abuse is coarse (வேசை முண்டைகள்). குன்றுகள் எங்கினுமே வளர்ந்தருள் makes Murugan lord of all hills. Some words (கடம்பிகள், மண்டைகள், லண்டிகள்) are abusive terms whose exact sense is unclear.

links.note: Both say the courtesan's sweet talk serves her wish for wealth, not love. The Kural states it as a warning; 180 shows the sequence, talk, trust, then the wealth snatched, and asks for the Lord's love in its place.

Both raise the breath from the root through the channel between ida and pingala to the head and arrive at the Lord's feet. Tirumular states the method; 188 asks for it as a gift, and hears the goal as the anklet sound of the dancing foot.

27 asks to see how to leave the embrace and gain the feet; 190 describes the same embrace and vows not to forget the feet even there. Read as a vow, 190 allows a remembrance inside desire that 27 seeks by leaving it.

The Tirumanthiram's verse is a chain of the Goddess's names, Tripura, Sundari, Narani, Manonmani, by which the one stands as many. 179 ends its namo-nama litany with the same names for Uma (மாதா மநோமணி ஆயி சுந்தரி தாயான நாரணி அபிராமி) as Murugan's mother. Worship by naming the Goddess is shared, and 179 sets it inside a hymn to her son.

Tirumular says people see the times of child, youth and old man pass (பாலன் இளையன் விருத்தன்) and still do not understand, and lies at the Lord's feet. 181 tells that life in stages, from being sent by Brahma to eat deeds through the breast and childhood to the grown man in common women's houses, and asks when he will worship the feet. The song fills in the Tirumanthiram's three stages with its own history.

The Tirumanthiram says the Veda and the Agama are both the true Lord's scripture and not different for the great. 182 asks to live in service without straying from the Manu texts, seeking the meaning the Vedas hold and following the Agamas in order (மிகுத்த பொருள் ஆகமங்கள் முறையாலே). The song turns the Tirumanthiram's doctrine of the two scriptures into a rule of conduct.

The Kural's lover says the girl's shoulders are made of nectar because each touch makes his life sprout anew (உயிர்தளிர்ப்ப ... அமிழ்தின் இயன்றன தோள்). 185 drinks the nectar of women's smiles (நகையமுதம்) and perishes by it (அழியும்), and asks to drink instead the nectar of the Lord's feet (இருதாளின் அமுது). On the plain reading the same nectar of love gives life in the Kural and death in the song.

The Naladiyar's renunciant refuses men who call eyes water-lilies, warring carp or spears (பொருகயல் வேல்) and sees the eye as a scooped palm fruit. 186 uses the same conceit of eyes outdoing deer, mango slice and carp (முதிய கயல்கள்) to describe the women whose eyes forced him into bondage. The figure the Naladiyar dismisses is the snare the song confesses.

The Tirumanthiram compares women who smile and display their breasts to the etti tree, fine in leaf and fruit but not to be eaten, and tells the heart to turn away. 187 lists a woman's ornaments in detail, then her sweet words, coral lips and poisonous eyes (நச்சுக்கண்), and asks whether he must go on wandering caught by them. Both set an adorned surface over harm.

The Tirumanthiram says no tapas is needed to make the mind Siva for one who has kinship with those whose minds have joined Siva's bliss (சிவானந்தம் சேர்ந்தோர் உறவு). 189 lists the mantra, giving, silence and jnana he lacks and asks for the keenness to join those of knowing heart (ஞான நெஞ்சினர் பால் இணங்கிடு கூர்மை). The song asks for the one remedy the Tirumanthiram says replaces the missing disciplines.

The Kural asks whether the lotus-eyed god's world is sweeter than sleep in the soft arms of the beloved (மென்றோள் துயிலின் இனிதுகொல்). 190 describes the same embrace and says that even sleeping on that bed (அமளி மலரணையின் மிசை துயிலுகினும்) he will not forget the lotus feet. The song keeps the Kural's sleep in love but refuses to let it displace the god.

The Naladiyar scorns blind, petty men who call women's eyes lilies, carp or spears. 191 confesses he was such a poet, describing hair as cloud, breasts as lotus buds, face as moon (உருவக உரைசெய்து), and melted like wax in a furnace in the union that followed. The song indicts its own craft in the terms the Naladiyar uses against the praisers.

The Naladiyar says bright-browed women hide harmful intent behind words spoken to be believed and belong to no one but their own bodies. 193 abuses women who talk of love without knowing friendship, never melt despite sweet words (இன்சொல் புரிந்து உருகாத) and attend only to the act of union. Both find the courtesan's speech a performance that hides an unmoved heart.

source_issues: Song 181: செறிவுடன் றிந்து (line 6) looks damaged, probably செறிவுடன் அறிந்து.
Song 179: ஆவல் கொண்டுவி றாலே சிராடவெ (line 22) is unclear and may be garbled.
Song 180: செந்தமிழ் லுனையே (line 21) is ungrammatical, probably செந்தமிழில் உனையே.
Song 192: ருளும்வோலா (line 6) is probably ருளும்வேலா, 'vel-bearer'; the letter is not flagged as corrupt.
